item.title: Observing the Future: Systems Theory Meets Science Fiction
item.content:encoded:
This special issue bridges systems theory and science fiction criticism to analyze speculative narratives as models of complex social systems. The editors argue that while science fiction commonly receives sociological interpretation, systematic application of Niklas Luhmann's theory and second-order cybernetics to the genre remains underexplored. The collection seeks to demonstrate how science fiction uniquely simulates social dynamics, including autopoiesis, operational closure, and functional differentiation, addressing contemporary concerns around artificial intelligence, fragmented discourse, and interconnected systems.

Appel publié par Kybernetes. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Investigations into the 'hypertrophy' of social subsystems (e.g., totalitarization of politics, economization of life) and dedifferentiation in utopian and dystopian literature
  • The emergence of non-human communicative systems, including Artificial Intelligence and alien consciousness, and their structural coupling with human society
  • Science fiction as a specific function of the art system, allowing society to observe its own evolution, paradoxes, and latent possibilities
  • Systems-theoretic readings of ecological crisis, the environment, and global interdependencies in speculative fiction
  • Examining the fragmentation of public discourse, 'echo chambers,' and the breakdown of communication through the lens of SF narratives

  • January 4, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • January 15, 2027: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: The Architecture of Meaning: Reconstructing Luhmann's Dimensional Framework
item.content:encoded:
Michal Kaczmarczyk, University of Gdańsk

Krešimir Žažar, University of Zagreb

Lars Clausen, University College London

This special issue examines Luhmann's concept of meaning as a central medium for both psychic and social systems, structured across three canonical dimensions: factual, temporal, and social. The call argues that while these three dimensions are foundational to systems theory, the underlying logic of why meaning should be organized into exactly these three dimensions remains unresolved. Recent scholarship suggests that meaning may be better understood as a potentially expandable framework responding to basic questions of observation, with additional dimensions such as spatial, modal, and motivational warranting exploration.

The special issue aims to revisit and extend meaning theory in response to contemporary societal complexities, particularly the technological mediation of meaning through artificial intelligence and algorithmic systems, as well as challenges like polarization and meaninglessness. It invites interdisciplinary contributions that employ reflexivity and second-order observation to explore how meaning is currently being observed, transformed, and contested across different media and inter-systemic relations.

Appel publié par Kybernetes. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Theoretical work revisiting or extending established three-dimensional models of meaning (factual, temporal, social), including introduction of novel distinctions such as spatial, modal, or motivational dimensions and expanded sub-programmes within systems theory
  • Studies focusing on second-order observation, reflexivity, and the inherent paradoxes of observation within social and psychic systems
  • Analyses of how artificial intelligence, artificial communication, and algorithmic decision premises impact meaning-processing systems, technological co-evolution, and structures of expectation
  • Explorations of forms of meaning that resist operational closure, reduction, or authoritarian simplification, including the role of imagination, counterfactuals, and non-necessary social orders
  • Systems-theoretical approaches to current societal challenges, encompassing values, political polarisation, populism, inter-systemic relations, strategies for complexity reduction, and pathologies of meaninglessness
  • Renewed theoretical and empirical engagement with sense-making, consciousness, psychology, and psychotherapy, with a focus on identity formation and the structural coupling between psychic and social systems

Timeline

  • September 21, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • December 13, 2026: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Explainable AI and Network Science for Social Systems and Collective Intelligence
item.content:encoded:
This special issue invites contributions that explore the intersection of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) and network science as applied to social systems and collective intelligence. The call seeks research that leverages both XAI methodologies and network science approaches to better understand, model, and explain complex social phenomena, emergent behaviors, and collective decision-making processes.

Appel publié par Information Processing & Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Applications of explainable AI in understanding social systems
  • Network science approaches to modeling collective intelligence
  • Integration of XAI and network methods for social analysis
  • Interpretability in multi-agent systems and social networks
  • Transparency and accountability in AI-driven social platforms
  • Graph-based methods for explaining collective behavior
  • Knowledge graphs and social network analysis
  • Fairness and bias detection in social AI systems

Timeline

  • March 31, 2027: Submission deadline
